transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi Dr. [Name]. I guess... what brings me in is that I just cannot keep my mind on one single thing anymore. I mean, I've been a carpenter for over thirty years, so I know my way around a woodshop, but lately it's just turning into a complete disaster. I'll be trying to focus on measuring a cut, and just one table saw starting up across the room, or even just somebody walking past the office window holding a piece of trim, and that's it, my attention is completely hijacked. I'm looking at them, wondering what they're working on, and I've completely lost my place. 

And it's not even just the noise or the guys in the shop, you know? Sometimes it's just my own brain betraying me. I'll be right in the middle of sanding down a beautiful piece of oak, and a thought about another job will just pop into my head—like whether I ordered the right hinges for that kitchen remodel across town—and that one little thought will pull me right off what I’m doing. I'll actually put my tools down to go check the invoice on the desk, but on the way there I'll see a stray pencil, start sharpening it, notice the trash needs emptying, take that out... and then the whole day just gets away from me. I'll look at the clock and it's suddenly 4:00 PM and I haven't gotten a single actual task finished. It's just exhausting, constantly getting derailed like that when I have deadlines to meet and clients waiting on me, and I just can't seem to stop every little thing from pulling me away.
How long have you been experiencing these attention problems? Did this start recently, or has this been going on for most of your life?

Well, see, that's the thing. I've always been a bit... you know, a bit scattered, maybe? Like, my husband used to joke that I could never just watch a movie without also knitting or doing a crossword puzzle. But this? This absolute inability to just get through a single day without my brain turning into a pinball machine? This is newer. 

I'd say it's been really, really bad for about... gosh, about a year and a month now. I know exactly when it started getting this severe because it was right after I broke my wrist. I was up on a ladder, installing some crown molding—beautiful stuff, real intricate profile, took me ages to mill it—and I just lost my footing. Clean break, right radius. Anyway, because I was in a cast and couldn't do the heavy lifting or run the big saws for a while, the boss moved me off the floor and put me in charge of the shop paperwork and supervising the younger guys. 

And let me tell you, that was when the wheels completely fell off the wagon. When I was just building cabinets or framing out a room, my hands were busy, you know? I could just lock into the physical work. But put me at a desk with a stack of invoices, material orders, and three different apprentices asking me questions every five minutes? It's like my brain just short-circuits. I'll sit down to review a lumber order, and I'll realize I haven't checked the inventory on wood glue, so I get up to do that, and then I see one of the kids using the wrong grit sandpaper on a finishing job, so I have to stop and correct him, and then I'll start telling him about this one time back in '98 when I ruined a whole dining table doing exactly what he's doing... and an hour later I haven't even looked at the lumber order. So yeah, it's been about thirteen months of this absolute chaos since I got stuck with the desk work. It's just a completely different world than being on the tools, and I just can't seem to handle it.
When you broke your wrist and were in the cast, did you have to take any pain medications or other medications during that time, and if so, are you still taking any of them now?

Oh, pain medications. Right, right. Well, you know, when it first happened, it hurt like the dickens. I mean, a clean break on the radius, that's your main bone there in the forearm, and I felt it snap. So they gave me something at the ER... um, I think it was one of those strong ones, maybe Vicodin or Percocet? I honestly don't remember the exact name, my husband was the one keeping track of the pill bottle because I was just in so much agony those first couple of days. 

But I didn't take them for very long. I really don't like the way those heavy painkillers make me feel, you know? They make my head all fuzzy and weird, and I was already feeling so out of sorts just being stuck on the couch with my arm propped up on a mountain of pillows, watching daytime television, which, let me tell you, is just dreadful. I couldn't stand being cooped up. So I think I only took the prescription stuff for maybe three or four days, tops, just to get through the absolute worst of the swelling and the throbbing. 

After that, I just switched over to regular over-the-counter stuff. Just ibuprofen, mostly. Advil. I'd take a couple of those in the morning with my coffee and maybe a couple more in the afternoon if it was really aching, especially when the weather would turn cold or damp. You know how old injuries ache when it rains? Well, it started doing that almost immediately. But as for now? No, no, I'm not taking anything for it anymore. The cast came off after six weeks, then I did a few weeks of physical therapy—which was a whole other ordeal, stretching those stiff tendons out, ouch—but the bone healed up beautifully. The doctor said I had great bone density for a woman my age, which I attribute to a lifetime of hauling lumber around! So no, I haven't taken any pain pills, prescription or otherwise, for... gosh, probably almost a year now. My wrist is perfectly fine, it's just my brain that's completely falling apart!

You mentioned your attention problems got much worse when you moved to the desk job. But I'm curious—when you're back doing the hands-on carpentry work now, or doing other activities you enjoy outside of work, do you find it easier to focus, or do you still struggle with distractions just as much?

Well, you know, that’s a really interesting question. I was actually just trying to figure that out myself the other day, because my husband—bless his heart—he noticed how stressed I’ve been and he went out and bought me these gorgeous rough-sawn cedar boards. Just beautiful wood, smells incredible. He knows I’ve been wanting to build some new raised planter boxes for the backyard for the tomatoes, and he figured getting my hands back on the tools at home, with no boss and no apprentices asking questions, would be relaxing for me. 

So I got out there on Saturday morning, set up my sawhorses on the patio, got my measuring tape out, and I was so ready to just sink into the work like I used to. But... gosh, I honestly don't even know if it was any easier. I really haven't noticed a difference, to tell you the truth. Because what happened was, I laid out the first board, and then I saw the garden hose was all tangled up in the corner of the yard. So I put my pencil down to go coil the hose properly—because you leave those things in the sun and they crack, you know—and while I was over there, I saw that the gutters had some leaves sticking out. So I went to the garage to get the ladder, but the garage was a mess, so I started organizing the recycling bins... and the next thing I know, my husband is calling me in for lunch and that beautiful cedar is just sitting there on the sawhorses, completely untouched. 

So to answer your question... I’m really not sure. I haven't really stopped to compare if the desk is strictly worse than the hands-on stuff nowadays, because it all just feels like a complete blur. Even with my knitting, which I’ve done for twenty years! I’ll sit down with a nice chunky wool yarn, do two rows, hear a car drive by, look out the window, remember I need to check the mail, and then the knitting just sits on the armchair for a week. 

So I really couldn't tell you if one is easier than the other at this point. I just know that whether I’m holding a clipboard, a circular saw, or a pair of knitting needles, my brain just will not let me stay put. Do people usually find one easier than the other? Because for me, it just feels like the exact same exhausting merry-go-round no matter where I am or what I'm doing. I mean, just yesterday I was trying to change the oil in the lawnmower, and I ended up cleaning out the birdbath instead, and I still don't know how that happened.

You mentioned you've always been a bit scattered, like with movies and knitting. But thinking back to your carpentry work before the wrist injury—when you were doing hands-on building work, were you able to focus and complete projects without getting distracted the way you do now, or were you struggling with attention even back then?

Well... you know, looking back, I think I might have been looking at my carpentry days through rose-colored glasses when I was talking about it earlier. Because if I really sit down and think about it... honestly, the struggle goes back so much further than the woodshop. I mean, way, way back. Even back in grade school, long before I was twelve years old, this was happening. 

I remember parent-teacher conferences were just an absolute ordeal for my poor mother. Every single year, it was the exact same broken record. My teachers—I remember Mrs. Gable in third grade specifically, she had these thick glasses that magnified her eyes and she'd lean over her desk—they were always, always telling my mother that I was a bright girl, but I was just so careless. That was the word they loved to use. Careless. 

I was constantly losing my homework. I’d sit at the kitchen table, do all the math problems, pack it up, and somehow between the front door and my desk at school, it would just vanish into thin air. And forgetting instructions! Oh my goodness, the teacher would stand at the chalkboard and give us three simple steps for an assignment, and by the time she finished speaking, my brain was already a million miles away. I'd just sit there, staring out the window at the playground, watching the wind blow through the oak trees or looking at the janitor sweeping the sidewalk, instead of finishing my seatwork like all the other kids in the room. 

So I guess... I guess the attention stuff has always been there, hasn't it? I think the hands-on building work just kind of masked it for a long time because I was physically moving around so much and using my hands, but that scattered little girl who couldn't finish her seatwork without looking out the window? She's really been there the whole time, right from the beginning.

opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with lifelong history of inattention, distractibility, and difficulty sustaining focus dating back to childhood (before age 12), with significant functional impairment across multiple domains (work, home, leisure activities). While symptoms worsened after the wrist injury and desk job transition approximately 13 months ago, the core attentional difficulties have persisted throughout her life and across all contexts (carpentry, desk work, hobbies, personal tasks). The pattern is consistent with ADHD, Combined or Predominantly Inattentive Type, with chronic course. No evidence of secondary causes (medication effects resolved, medical workup not indicated by history). F90.9 (Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, unspecified) is appropriate given the lifelong presentation and pervasive functional impairment.
